title: Part I — MARKETPLACE: The Business Behind the Listings
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published page (posts/part-1-intro/index.md) and its former spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces; one spec paragraph per unit of the page, in the page's order. Intent outcome, AC-1 to AC-3 and role are copied unchanged from the post's entry in journal-spec.json; the introduction realises Part I's opening (hook, bridge, roadmap) from the same file. The journal spec gives this post no thesis, so the thesis and its two supporting claims are written here from the part's thesis and flow. The five callouts (IN THIS PART, WHY THE BUSINESS CARES, WHY ARCHITECTS SHOULD CARE, KEY POINTS, FAILURE PATTERNS) stand before the first paragraph and are kept as the house format; the KEY POINTS callout carries the part's claim in three bullets. Three units were added to the published page to meet the contract: the roadmap paragraph (p03), the lead-in to the chapter table (p04) and the closing paragraph (p07, which grew from the one-line pointer 'Begin with [[marketplace-taxonomy]]').

know: Part I answers six questions in order: what kind of marketplace this is, what it sells, how the industry formed, what the marketplace does, where the boundaries go and how verticals differ.

thesis.question: What does this part argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?
thesis.claim: Part I argues that in a listing marketplace the business decides the architecture before any technology choice, and its six chapters are read in a fixed order because each answer is the vocabulary the next question needs: the marketplace model, then liquidity, then the industry's history, then capabilities, bounded contexts and vertical profiles, which together are the business facts every later boundary, target and shared platform must name.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a marketplace group's platform decisions start from its systems inventory and the strongest brand's stack, so the business chapters are background a reader may skip or read in any order.
thesis.so_what: A reader who accepts it reads Part I before the platform chapters, or opens the one chapter that answers the decision in front of them, and expects every later freshness, latency and sharing decision to point back to this part's liquidity metrics and share test.
thesis.how_why: The model decides what liquidity is measured on; liquidity's local network effects explain why groups are portfolios of local leaders; that history shows why a systems inventory cannot be the unit for comparing brands, so capabilities are; the capability map is the input to the bounded contexts; and the vertical profiles ask where the sameness of those maps stops.

supporting_claims.claim: The six chapters answer six questions in an order where each answer supplies the next question's vocabulary, and each is the chapter to open first for a recognizable situation.

The part's vocabulary (marketplace profile, liquidity cell, capability, bounded context, vertical requirement profile) is what the rest of the book justifies its boundaries, targets and shared platforms with.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states that the business decides the architecture, the reading order of the six chapters and what Veldmark decides in them.

flow.rationale: The page opens on the part's claim (the business model decides the architecture), narrows to the three pieces of business knowledge a sharing decision needs, then to the six questions that supply them in order (two, one and three chapters per piece), then to one row per chapter with the situation in which to open it. It then widens once to place the part's vocabulary in the book, and ends on Veldmark, where the same vocabulary becomes dated decisions, followed by a short synthesis that hands off to the first chapter. The roadmap stands before the table because the table's rows only make sense as answers to questions the reader already has; the connection section follows the table because it names the vocabulary the chapters define; Veldmark comes last in the body of the conclusion because its decisions use that vocabulary; the synthesis follows it so the page's last words are the first chapter's question. Put Veldmark first and its profiles, cells and contexts arrive before the reader knows they are the part's terms; put the connection first and it names a vocabulary no chapter has yet been shown to supply. The six questions follow the three pieces of knowledge because they are those pieces divided into chapters; put the questions first and the reader holds six items with no grouping.

hook.content: This book starts with the business, not the systems, because in a listing marketplace the business model decides the architecture: a classifieds site whose job ends at the contact, a portal that sells qualified leads and a marketplace that holds buyers' money need different identity, trust, payment and data systems, even when their search pages look alike.

evidence.shows: Three marketplaces that look alike from the search page need different systems beneath it, so the model, not the page, decides the architecture.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Deciding what a group like Veldmark should share takes three pieces of business knowledge, supplied in order: what kind of marketplace it is and what it sells, which is liquidity (glossed); how the industry got here, since buyers go where sellers already are, so each country and category ended up with one leader, groups bought such leaders and each brand still runs the systems of the industry wave it was built in; and what the marketplace does, where its boundaries go and how its verticals differ, described in terms that outlive systems and reorganizations.

evidence.shows: The part is the foundation every later system decision rests on, in the six pieces the chapters supply.
